rationale: Both avoid private-memory retrieval, but B's bounded choice-function interface is the smaller intervention. A adds response lattices, a VM, split transcripts, a continuity compiler, local smoothing, receipts, and learning machinery before proving that simpler local ranking and late binding are insufficient.

A earns a narrow preference by making the core runtime deterministic, removing personalized feedback, limiting the first prototype to three task families, and stating quantitative kill criteria. B is clear but layers an ABI, evidence objects, three disclosure modes, local transformations, receipts, and cumulative disclosure accounting without an equally sharp minimal prototype.

A's one-way Answer Bytecode and Memory Test VM is already substantial, but B adds a Task Contract, local verifier, counterfactual egress gate, sink-specific delivery, and disclosure receipts. Those additions improve breadth yet stack complexity before the simpler output-selection hypothesis is validated.

Both correctly buffer only the dry-rejection deficit and expose the costs. A is simpler because it keeps workload scheduling secondary and uses conventional sensible storage plus mechanical fallback; B adds a facilities-to-cluster thermal-headroom market whose benefit should be demonstrated separately.

B explicitly removes PCM in favor of inspectable stratified-water storage and sizes mechanical trim to the residual deficit. A requires thousands of tonnes of specialty PCM while retaining full mechanical backup, so the extra material, lifecycle risk, and maintenance are not justified over B's simpler substitute.

B chooses the straightforward dry-first series cascade with residual refrigeration and only short ride-through storage. A's water-plus-PCM flywheel is more differentiated but adds tanks, latent modules, recharge dependence, and controls when a conventional high-temperature dry cooler plus trim chiller directly satisfies the freshwater objective.

Both replace profile browsing with bottleneck-level dispatch. B keeps one coherent Resolution Relay mechanism, whereas A adds misconception pooling, multiple intake surfaces, extensive session infrastructure, a resolution map, and several settlement features before validating whether bottleneck-specific routing alone beats ordinary matching.

The mechanisms are very close. A wins narrowly because it specifies a one-subject, 20–30-tutor MVP, keeps outcome pay bounded, and preregisters a comparison against ordinary matching. B communicates the product more cleanly but proposes six services and portable impact receipts without an equally decisive minimal test.

B centers the product on packetized bottleneck dispatch and expert relay. A combines mastery escrow, continuity capsules, intervention fingerprints, transfer probes, credentials, and payment-dependent assessment; that stack is harder to operate and not necessary to test whether transition-specific routing is useful.

A uses an ordinary cycler plus a simple force fixture and reduces the observable to loading/unloading hysteresis after rejecting full EIS. B avoids the mechanical fixture but requires high-rate low-noise acquisition and elaborate residual-event statistics for a notably more speculative microbridge signal. A also provides the cleaner causal falsifier.

B uses one PZT patch and synchronous cross-modulation around a selected resonance. A requires two transducers, baseline spectra, charge-neutral pulse pairs in both orders, nuisance correction, and reciprocity subtraction. Its validation is excellent, but the instrumentation and protocol exceed what is necessary for the first causal test.

B explicitly abandons current-to-stress spectroscopy after identifying direct prior art and substitutes two matched pulses plus a mechanical null residual. A retains broadband excitation, transfer spectra, coherence, two amplitudes, and nonlinear features. B tests essentially the same defect hypothesis with much less apparatus and analysis.

Both correctly eliminate duplicate authorship through evidence resolution and exception-only teacher input. B is marginally stronger because it starts with one report and two or three read-only connections, fixes quantitative proceed/stop thresholds, and keeps facts deterministic. A's sunset rule is valuable but its eight-layer presentation is slightly broader than necessary for the first proof.

The proposals are nearly equivalent. B more explicitly tests report abolition and live views as substitutes, compresses the implementation to six layers, and starts with one high-burden workflow and a few sources. A's obligation graph is useful but adds semantic-deduplication machinery before the core once-only compiler is proven.

B's Reuse/Derive/Ask/Delete rule is a smaller and more operational control policy than A's broader semantic evidence architecture. It also defines a one-report prototype, an explicit 20%-of-baseline time gate, and a clear fallback to report-scope reduction. A is sound but less decisively testable.

Both correctly stop at conservation of energy rather than inventing a hidden source. B states the boundary equation, dispatches the main loopholes, and ends sooner. A is equally correct but spends more text on nearby mechanisms without changing the conclusion.

B gives the conservation equation, a compact loophole audit, and the smallest constraint change that opens a legitimate invention space. A's four-family portfolio, assumption graph, anti-fake-novelty section, and innovation-delta analysis are accurate but unnecessary for this direct law-level contradiction.

Both are physically correct. A reaches the no-go with a compact first-law argument and only enough frontier discussion to close plausible loopholes. B's longer mechanism table and separate assumption and anti-fake-novelty sections add little decision value.

B directly pools paid time-bounded availability options across restaurants. A's productive preemptible reserve is more inventive but requires interruptible task inventories, worker rerouting between employers, standardized cross-training, travel clearing, credits, and a four-market system. That operational stack should not precede testing the simpler standby-capacity pool.

Both converge on pooled paid reserve capacity. B expresses the product more economically as a coverage contract with fractional reserve, four bounded agents, and positive worker compensation. A adds a trust agent, reciprocal passports, hiring-fee stabilization guarantees, and a three-market structure that are not needed to test the pooling mechanism.

A already supplies the essential primary-plus-pooled-reserve coverage contract and recognizes that blockchain should disappear if federation never materializes. B adds a secondary transfer market, coverage underwriting, temp-to-hire, four agents, multi-market settlement, and a larger launch stack. Its thresholds are excellent, but the combined mechanism is overbuilt for the first pooling test.

Both correctly make paper authoritative and reject a new mechanism. B is slightly simpler operationally: two half-days, three capacity buckets, two visit sizes, and four tally boxes. A's three-band priority and spillover policy is useful but more rule-heavy without a demonstrated need.

B uses visible boxes, one-in-five reserve, and only conditionally adds a two-box long-visit rule. A requires four windows, three workload weights, a patient-level spreadsheet mirror, and several handling rules. B more cleanly avoids duplicate entry and specifies when even its optional refinements should be removed.

B keeps ordinary paper slots, shortens the booking horizon, protects same-day capacity, makes arrival bands conditional, and records only weekly aggregate tallies. A mandates hourly blocks, workload boxes, per-block daily tallies, and two visit sizes. Those refinements may help, but B better obeys the instruction to add mechanism only when local evidence requires it.
